{pipeflow} computes the results of an analysis in pipeline steps. {pubflow}
adds what you need to *publish* these results:

* **parameters** that describe themselves (label, limits, description) and
  check their values;
* **outputs** for documents: tables, figures and text;
* **documents** that steps of the pipeline build from these outputs;
* **reports** in HTML, Word and PDF format;
* **Shiny modules** for a parameter UI and a document viewer.

This vignette goes through all of them with one small example. It assumes
that you know how to build and run a pipeline; if not, read pipeflow's
[Get started](https://cran.r-project.org/package=pipeflow/vignettes/v01-get-started.html)
first.

## The example

We use the example of pipeflow's Get started vignette: a pipeline that
adds a temperature column in degrees Celsius to base R's `airquality` data,
fits a linear model of the ozone concentration and plots the fit.

```{r pipeline}
library(pipeflow)

pip <- pip_new("my-pip") |>
    pip_add("data", function(data = airquality) data) |>
    pip_add("prep", function(df = ~data) {
        df[, "Temp.Celsius"] <- (df[, "Temp"] - 32) * 5 / 9
        df
    }) |>
    pip_add("fit", function(data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        lm(paste("Ozone ~", xVar), data = data)
    })
```

To publish the results, we add three things: params that describe the
pipeline's parameters, steps that turn the results into a table, a figure and
a text, and a step that arranges them into a document.

## Parameters

A pipeflow parameter is a plain R value, the default of a step function's
argument. A pubflow parameter (a *param*) is a value with attributes that
describe it: a label, limits, a description, and so on. A *param config*
collects the params of an analysis:

```{r config}
library(pubflow)

config <- param_config(
    xVar = choice_param(
        "Temp.Celsius",
        choices = c("Temp.Celsius", "Wind", "Solar.R"),
        label = "Predictor",
        source = "user",
        description = "Variable that explains the ozone concentration"
    ),
    level = numeric_param(
        0.95,
        label = "Confidence level",
        min = 0.5,
        max = 0.999,
        source = "user"
    ),
    title = param(
        "Ozone in New York",
        label = "Report title",
        source = "user"
    )
)
config
```

Each kind of param checks its values: `choice_param()` allows only one of
its `choices` (its value is a factor), `numeric_param()` only a number
between `min` and `max`. `source = "user"` marks the params that the user
sets, so that an app or a report can pick them out.

## Outputs

The next steps turn the results into outputs that a document can show:
`pub_table()` makes a table with column labels and the number of decimal
places, `pub_figure()` a figure with a caption, and `pub_text()` a text in
Markdown.

```{r output-functions}
library(ggplot2)

coef_table <- function(model, level) {
    ci <- confint(model, level = level)
    coefs <- data.frame(
        term = rownames(ci),
        estimate = coef(model),
        lower = ci[, 1L],
        upper = ci[, 2L]
    )
    pub_table(
        coefs,
        caption = sprintf("Coefficients with %g%% confidence limits", 100 * level),
        labels = c(
            term = "Term",
            estimate = "Estimate",
            lower = "Lower",
            upper = "Upper"
        ),
        digits = c(estimate = 3L, lower = 3L, upper = 3L)
    )
}

fit_figure <- function(model, data, xVar) {
    coefs <- coef(model)
    p <- ggplot(data, aes(.data[[xVar]], .data$Ozone)) +
        geom_point(na.rm = TRUE) +
        geom_abline(intercept = coefs[[1L]], slope = coefs[[2L]])
    pub_figure(p, caption = "Linear model fit", width = 6, height = 3.5)
}
```

```{r output-steps}
pip |>
    pip_add("coef_table", function(model = ~fit, level = 0.95) {
        coef_table(model, level)
    }) |>
    pip_add("plot", function(model = ~fit, data = ~prep, xVar = "Temp.Celsius") {
        fit_figure(model, data, as.character(xVar))
    }) |>
    pip_add("summary", function(model = ~fit) {
        r2 <- summary(model)$r.squared
        pub_text(sprintf(
            "The model explains **%.0f%%** of the variance of the ozone concentration.",
            100 * r2
        ))
    })
```

The table and the figure are made by functions defined outside the pipeline
(here `coef_table()` and `fit_figure()`). This matters for figures: a ggplot
keeps the environment it was made in, so a plot made inside the pipeline's
code would keep the pipeline alive in every copy of the figure.

## A document

The last step is a *layout step*: it takes the outputs of other steps and
arranges them into a document with `pub_doc()` and `pub_section()`.

```{r layout-step}
pip |>
    pip_add(
        "report",
        function(
            title = "",
            summary = ~summary,
            table = ~coef_table,
            plot = ~plot
        ) {
            pub_doc(
                pub_section("Results", summary, table, plot),
                title = title
            )
        }
    )
```

Finally, we set the params of the config in the pipeline. Each param goes to
every step that has an argument of its name, here `xVar` to the steps `fit`
and `plot`:

```{r set-params}
pip_set_params(pip, config)
pip
```

The steps still get plain values: `coef_table` gets `level = 0.95`, not the
param object. `pub_get_params()` reads the params back from the pipeline:

```{r get-params}
names(pub_get_params(pip))
```

## Run and view

We run the pipeline and take the document from the output of the layout step:

```{r run}
pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
doc <- pip[["report", "out"]]
doc
```

`pub_html()` renders the document to HTML. In an R Markdown document like this
vignette, the HTML is shown in place:

```{r html, eval = FALSE}
pub_html(doc)
```

```{r html-framed, echo = FALSE}
# The same, framed to set it apart from the vignette's own text, and with
# its headings left out of the table of contents of the pkgdown site
html <- pub_html(doc)
htmltools::div(
    style = "border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 4px; padding: 0 1em;",
    htmltools::attachDependencies(
        htmltools::HTML(gsub("<h([1-6])", "<h\\1 data-toc-skip", html)),
        htmltools::htmlDependencies(html)
    )
)
```

## Change a param

Params are set with pipeflow's `pip_set_params()`. pubflow checks the new
value against the param's rules before it is set:

```{r set-valid}
pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Solar.R"))
pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
pip[["coef_table", "out"]]
```

An invalid value is an error, and nothing is set:

```{r set-invalid, error = TRUE}
pip_set_params(pip, list(xVar = "Height"))
pip_set_params(pip, list(level = 1.5))
```

## A report file

`pub_render()` writes the document to a file with pandoc: a Word document, a
PDF (via LaTeX or Typst) or Markdown. The metadata given at render time
appear in the document, e.g. the author:

```{r render-docx}
file <- pub_render(doc, "docx", meta = list(author = "Jane Doe"))
basename(file)
```

By default, the file goes to R's temporary directory, and its name is made of
the render time and the title. A PDF needs a LaTeX installation (xelatex) or
typst:

```{r render-pdf, eval = FALSE}
pub_render(doc, "pdf", file = "ozone.pdf")
pub_render(doc, "pdf", file = "ozone.pdf", pdf_engine = "typst")
```

`pub_report_spec()` sets up the format of a report: page size and margins, a
title page, a Word template, and more.

## A Shiny app

Two Shiny modules turn the pipeline into an app: `pub_params_ui()` with
`pub_pipeline_params_server()` shows an input for every param of the pipeline
and sets the values that the user enters in the pipeline, and `pub_viewer_ui()`
with `pub_viewer_server()` shows the document.

```{r shiny, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)

ui <- fluidPage(
    fluidRow(
        column(4, pub_params_ui("params")),
        column(8, pub_viewer_ui("viewer", height = "90vh"))
    )
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
    pip <- pip_clone(pip) # every session gets its own pipeline
    params <- pub_pipeline_params_server("params", pip)
    doc <- reactive({
        params$revision() # run again after every change of a param
        pip_run(pip, lgr = NULL)
        pip[["report", "out"]]
    })
    pub_viewer_server("viewer", doc)
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

An invalid input is marked and the last valid value is restored, so the
pipeline only ever gets valid values. A pipeline is a reference object, so
`server()` starts with a copy (`pip_clone()`): otherwise a change of a param
in one session would also change the pipeline of every other session.

The report app that comes with pubflow shows more: grouped params, two
reports from one pipeline, failed steps in the document and the download of
the report. Run it with

```{r report-app, eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(system.file("examples", "report-app", package = "pubflow"))
```

The help pages of the functions used here describe them in detail:

* params: `?param`, `?param_config`, `?param_validity`, `?pub_get_params`;
* outputs: `?pub_table`, `?pub_figure`, `?pub_text`;
* documents: `?pub_doc`, `?pub_layout_inputs`;
* rendering and reports: `?pub_html`, `?pub_render`, `?pub_report_spec`;
* Shiny: `?pub_params_ui`, `?pub_viewer_ui`.
